lines.text: a graph is not a diagram — it is a set of relationships
lines.note: a graph cannot supply its own abstraction — someone must rule first that the stone, the toll and the river are not part of a crossing; Euler's impossibility is exact only because everything that made the walk hard was already thrown away.

lines.text: graph theory begins when you stop asking "which route should I try?" and ask "what does the structure allow at …
Watch a tangled graph draw itself. Springs pull linked nodes together while repulsion pushes every pair apart
lines.note: a graph has no coordinates, so it must borrow a body — Coulomb's repulsion, Hooke's springs — from a physics that has never heard of the relation it is drawing; change the seed and the centre moves.

lines.text: pathfinding does not move through space — it moves through a graph that happens to be embedded in space
lines.note: A* beats exhaustive search only because someone hands it a distance the graph does not contain — h(n) is imported from the embedding, and when the embedding lies the confident path is the wrong one.

lines.text: a rhizome has no beginning and no end — only middles
lines.note: the rhizome that refuses every root must still be grown from one — each node buds from a random parent, and lateral edges only hide the tree afterwards; at connection_probability 0 the anti-hierarchy is a hierarchy.

lines.text: Read a network as hierarchy, community, and circulation at once
maximum flow through a network equals the minimum cut that separates source from sink
Topological sort — linear ordering of vertices in a directed acyclic graph
lines.note: an order exists only where nothing loops back — the cycles must be contracted to points before the sort can run, so a sequence costs every mutual reachability inside it, and the snarl that will not condense stands aside, unsorted.

lines.text: a strongly connected component is a pocket of mutual reachability
Kosaraju's algorithm proves that strongly connected components are the same in a graph and its transpose

pearls.edge: you place the nodes and believe you drew the graph, but an edge needs a threshold — the room holds a radius for what counts as near, never shows it, and every relation you think you made was already ruled.

lines.text: the minimum spanning tree is the cheapest way to keep everyone connected
lines.note: minimum needs a number the graph never had: weight comes from outside, and a different cost function grows a different tree from the same nodes — the cycles it rejects were the only alternative route anything had.

lines.text: Karger's algorithm is a bet that randomness repeated enough times becomes certainty
push-relabel proves that maximum flow can be found without ever finding a complete path
lines.note: flow only runs downhill and a graph has no down — push-relabel must invent an altitude, seeding the source at |V| and raising any node that gets stuck, so the gradient carrying everything is a bookkeeping number.

lines.text: matching is the mathematics of pairing — who connects with whom
lines.note: an odd cycle cannot pair itself — match any two and a third is stranded, so the blossom's completion must come from outside it; the greedy pass shipped here never looks outside, and calls its leftovers structural.
